citation: Schwitzgebel E, McVey C, May J (2022). Engaging charitable giving: the motivational force of narrative versus philosophical argument. Philosophical Psychology. doi:10.1080/09515089.2022.2088340 (author final manuscript, faculty.ucr.edu/~eschwitz/SchwitzPapers/EngagingCharitableGiving-MS.pdf)
arm_label: Narrative (N) vs physics control (C)
country: USA (MTurk, US-only workers)
treatment_description: Narrative only: the 'Mamtha' story, copied verbatim from the International Justice Mission charity website (a ten-year-old girl whose family is tricked into slavery in a sand mine is freed through a charity-funded rescue and is now studying to be a doctor); same texts as Exp 1
control_description: Physics control: 'a portion of a middle school physics text on the nature of energy' (p. 8)
outcome_description: Pledged donation (USD 0-10 in $1 steps) out of an additional $10 that 10% of participants would receive (lottery); donation directed to one of six charities (e.g. Against Malaria Foundation, Feeding America)
location: p. 23 (Section 3.2, Experiment 2 donation results)
notes: SD is the pooled SD reported for this N vs C pair (used for sd_t and sd_c). Preregistered one-tailed pairwise t = 2.42, p = .008; df not reported. Per-condition n not reported: total included N = 917 across four conditions (N, NA, A, C). In the 4-group ANOVA (pooled SD 3.24, F[3, 913] = 4.99) Tukey found NA > C only; 'the narrative condition alone was not statistically significantly different from ... the control condition' (p. 22). Random assignment: Exp 2 'identical to Experiment 1' where participants 'were randomly assigned'. Preregistered on OSF. Donation is the primary outcome ('Our primary concern is with the effect of narratives versus arguments on real charitable giving', p. 18). Incentivized via 10% lottery of $10; the paper states the donated portion 'will be given to the charity you pick' (p. 19) but never confirms transfers were made. Only pooled SDs are reported; per-condition n is not reported (no table gives it). Narrative is a true modern charity story (coded modern_invented). Exp 1 not recorded: hypothetical donation (not incentivized) and not preregistered. Argument-only arms belong to stratum N and are not recorded here. Attitude outcome not recorded (not behaviour). Email sign-up not recorded (not incentivized giving).

citation: Rand DG, Dreber A, Haque OS, Kane RJ, Nowak MA, Coakley S (2014). Religious motivations for cooperation: an experimental investigation using explicit primes. Religion, Brain & Behavior 4:31-48. doi:10.1080/2153599X.2013.775664 (author PDF via daverand.squarespace.com)
arm_label: Christian prime vs neutral prime, Christian subjects
country: International MTurk sample (full sample: 278 US, 197 India, 72 elsewhere); residence of Christian subjects not reported
treatment_description: Christian prime: Gospel of Mark passage on charity (Mark 10:17-23, a man asks Jesus what he must do to inherit eternal life), same passage as Study 1
control_description: Neutral prime: non-religious passage describing three fish species (Flounder, Jack, Triple Tail); 'A Flounder is a fish with a brown body.'
outcome_description: Cooperation (1) vs defection (0) in a one-shot prisoner's dilemma for real money (payoffs in cents: both cooperate 120/120, sucker 40/160, both defect 80/80), ex post matching with other MTurk workers; logistic regression
location: p. 41, Table 4 (Christians column); n from Figure 2 labels (p. 39)
notes: text: 'the positive effect of the Christian prime on cooperation is significant (p.037)' (p. 38; the comparison symbol before .037 is lost in the text layer); sign positive per text. Study 2 only (Study 1 compared two Bible passages with no neutral control). N = 547 MTurk workers 'from around the world', randomly assigned to four priming conditions (neutral n = 158, Christian n = 123, Hindu n = 131, secular n = 135, p. 37). Results are reported only within religious subgroups: logistic regressions with robust SEs, neutral prime as baseline, controls for female, age, age squared, belief in God, US residence, education, income (Tables 4-5, p. 41). No pooled full-sample test is reported; condition cooperation rates appear only as bars in Figure 2 (not read). b is in log-odds; sd_y not applicable (binary outcome; overall cooperation 0.298, SD 0.458, Table 2). n_t and n_c are the subgroup-by-condition sample sizes printed in Figure 2; the regression Ns (Christians 227, Hindus 120, Atheists 96) are smaller than the Figure 2 totals (229, 141, 96), so arm ns in the regressions are not reported. Partners: 'interacted with other strangers on the MTurk system' (p. 43). Decision made in the same session after reading and summarizing the passage, PD instructions and five comprehension questions. Preregistration not mentioned. SIGN CAUTION: the PDF text layer drops minus signs and '<'/'=' symbols (e.g. 'p.037'); coefficients were read from that text layer, so signs not corroborated by the paper's text should be checked against the printed table.

citation: Lombardi E, Valle A, Rinaldi T, Massaro D, Marchetti A (2021). Learning to wait and be altruistic: testing a conversational training in economic education for primary school children. Europe's Journal of Psychology 17(4):306-318. doi:10.5964/ejop.2453
arm_label: Training group (TG) vs control group (CG)
country: Italy (two schools, Northern Italy near Milan)
treatment_description: Conversational training in economic education: three one-hour in-class sessions run by a researcher on fairness, altruism and delayed gratification; each topic used two stories (invented or from Varela 2014 / Larsen et al. 2017), each story followed by four multiple-choice questions and group discussion
control_description: Control group 'only attended civics education classes, established in their state curricula' (p. 308); no-text control (flag per protocol)
delay: delayed: post-test one week after the end of the three training sessions
outcome_description: Dictator game: number of 10 trading cards given to a passive player, 'a schoolmate depicted in a drawing' (unnamed); score 0-10; one round, real cards
quote: children in the TG showed significantly higher post-test offers compared to the post-test offers in the CG, F(1, 108) = 5.431, p = .022
location: p. 310 (Results, Dictator Game)
notes: F is the pairwise group comparison at post-test from the repeated-measures GLM with covariate (eta2 = .071); sign 1 because the paper states TG offers were higher than CG at post-test. Recipient is an unnamed schoolmate in a drawing ('hypothetical - but well defined', p. 311), coded ingroup. N = 110 children aged 8-10 (TG n = 55, CG n = 55) from six 3rd-5th grade classes in two schools near Milan. Assignment by class: 'Two classes for each age range participated and for every range one class was randomly assigned to the CG' (p. 308), i.e. cluster randomization. Pre-test, training one week later, post-test 'one week after training sessions end'. Repeated-measures GLM with time within, group between, verbal ability as covariate (groups differed at pre-test only on verbal ability). No group x time interaction statistic is reported. Means/SDs appear only in Figure 1 (DG, values not printed) and in supplementary Appendix 2 (not opened). 'Decision making tasks were played for real, giving a final amount of trading cards' (p. 309). No outcome is designated primary. Treatment adds questions and discussion to the stories and also targets delayed gratification. Ultimatum game results are reported only as within-group pre/post McNemar tests (not a treatment vs control comparison; UG not a P outcome) and are not recorded. Preregistration not mentioned.

citation: Li Q, Li N (2024). Social media and adolescents' prosocial behavior: evidence of the interaction between short videos and social value orientation. Psychology Research and Behavior Management 17:3267-3281. doi:10.2147/PRBM.S469641
arm_label: Prosocial short videos vs neutral short videos
country: China (two secondary schools, Shanghai)
treatment_description: Watched three prosocial short videos found on TikTok, Weibo and Bilibili by searching 'help' and 'kindness' (e.g. strangers helping the elderly, drivers returning lost wallets)
control_description: Watched three neutral short videos (searches 'travel' and 'scenery'); 'neutral short videos do not involve interpersonal interaction' (p. 3270)
outcome_description: Amount donated (0-15 RMB) 'from a bonus fund' to a real online charity for children in impoverished areas (rainbowforlove.org); authors state 'we will directly transfer the money to the charity organization'
location: p. 3272, Table 1 (Descriptive Statistics), prosocial behavior row
notes: t = 7.70 (Table 1). n per content condition not printed in Table 1; n_t and n_c summed from the reported cells (prosocial video: 39 prosocial-SVO + 35 pro-self; neutral: 39 + 35; p. 3271). Valid N = 148 adolescents, mean age 16.29 (coded children). Random assignment 'by randomly drawing group cards' (p. 3271); SVO measured, not assigned (2 x 2 design). INCONSISTENCY: the text reports different means for the same contrast, 'significant main effects of short video content, F(1, 147)=152.64, p<0.001' with prosocial M = 9.63 (SD = 2.48) vs neutral M = 5.60 (SD = 2.24) (p. 3271; sign 1, prosocial higher); Table 1 values recorded because the t-test is a direct two-group comparison. Simple effects by SVO (no test statistics): prosocial SVO 12.54 (3.02) vs 6.88 (3.25), n 39/39; pro-self 5.45 (2.34) vs 4.74 (1.82), n 35/35. Cost to participants unclear: they received a fixed 15 RMB participation fee and the paper does not say whether undonated bonus money was kept. Donation measured after the manipulation check in the same session. Study 2 not recorded: it compares reward vs punishment versions of the same prosocial videos with no neutral control. Preregistration not mentioned.
